description: We are an interdisciplinary team of data scientists, bioinformaticians, and software engineers with expertise in data analysis, AI/ML, scientific computing, and software development. For NASA Space Apps, we combine our skills to analyze Earth observation data, detect environmental trends, and build an accessible solution that transforms complex data into meaningful insights. We welcome Earth scientists, GIS experts, environmental researchers, and web developers to strengthen our team.
summary:
Earth System Detective is a web app that helps students, scientific audience and the public find, test and explain trends in Earth-system data. Users choose a place (any country or region), a period and variables, or simply ask a question in plain English or French. An AI assistant (Gemini, with a keyword-based fallback) turns the question into an analysis plan the user confirms.

The app downloads NASA data (MODIS vegetation, land temperature and fire; NASA POWER temperature and rainfall from MERRA-2 and GPM IMERG), plus TerraClimate and ERA5, through the Microsoft Planetary Computer STAC API. It summarises them within real country borders. It then visualises the series, measures each trend (least squares with confidence intervals, plus Mann-Kendall and Sen's slope), and states whether it is statistically significant.

Users can compare zones and variables, map hotspots of change, and forecast the coming months with uncertainty bands. Every result carries caveats and avoids causal claims. Example: over 1981–2025, The Gambia warmed by about 0.09 °C per decade and gained about 47 mm of yearly rainfall per decade; both trends are significant.
details:
superNasaDetector: Be an Earth System Trend Detective (Team DOUBLE HELIX)

What it does and how it works

superNasaDetector is a web app that answers four questions about any place on Earth: what is changing, where, by how much, and is the change real or just noise?

  1. Choose a place and a variable. Pick a country, a region, or draw a box on the map. Then choose from NASA MODIS (vegetation/NDVI, land surface temperature, fire), NASA POWER (rainfall, air temperature) and other climate data (TerraClimate, ERA5). You can also just type a question, such as "Has rainfall changed in The Gambia since 1981?" An AI assistant pulls out the place, the variable and the years, shows you its plan, and runs the analysis.
  2. Get the data. The app downloads the data from the Microsoft Planetary Computer and the NASA POWER API, and averages it inside the real country border. You can work month by month, day by day, or (for ERA5) hour by hour.
  3. Test the trend. We measure how fast each variable changes per decade. Two tests check whether the trend is real: Mann-Kendall with Sen's slope (which resists outliers), and a linear trend with a confidence interval. The app says "significant" only when p < 0.05. Otherwise it says "no clear trend".
  4. See where it changes. Hotspot maps colour every grid cell of a country by its average value or its trend, and point out the highest and lowest areas.
  5. Compare and forecast. You can compare several regions and several variables at once. Machine-learning models (SARIMA, Holt-Winters, Ridge, Random Forest, LightGBM) compete to forecast the next months. The winner is shown only if it beats simple rules such as "same month last year".

Example result (The Gambia).

  • Rainfall has risen by about 47 mm/year per decade since 1981 (p = 0.016).
  • Air temperature has risen by 0.09 °C per decade (p = 0.017).
  • Vegetation (2001–2024) shows no clear trend.
  • The south-west gets about 96 mm/month of rain, the north-east about 59.
  • For the rainfall forecast, SARIMA was 14% more accurate than the simple rule "same month last year".

Benefits

  • One tool goes from raw NASA satellite data to a clear, tested answer in minutes. Nothing to install, and no coding needed.
  • Plain-language questions and results, in English or French.
  • Honest output: it reports significance and flags data that is too short. It describes links between variables as associations, not causes.
  • Results can be saved and exported as CSV for further work.

Intended impact

We want NASA Earth data to be useful to people who are not remote-sensing experts:

  • Farmers and communities can see how rainfall and heat are shifting where they live.
  • Students can learn data science with real climate data.
  • Researchers can screen many variables and regions quickly.
  • Policy makers get clear evidence, with uncertainty stated, to support decisions on agriculture, water and climate adaptation.

We started with The Gambia, a country very exposed to rainfall change, but the tool works for any country or region.

Tools, languages, hardware and software

  • Languages: Python, JavaScript, HTML/CSS.
  • Backend: FastAPI, Jinja2.
  • Data and science libraries:
    • pandas, NumPy, SciPy, xarray;
    • GDAL/rasterio, Shapely/GeoPandas;
    • statsmodels, scikit-learn, LightGBM, pymannkendall.
  • Frontend: Leaflet for maps, Plotly for charts.
  • Data sources:
    • NASA MODIS through the Microsoft Planetary Computer;
    • the NASA POWER API;
    • TerraClimate and ERA5.
  • AI: Google Gemini API, with our own keyword parser as a backup that needs no internet AI service.
  • Development and deployment: Jupyter notebooks, conda, Git/GitHub, Vercel for the lightweight online version.
  • Hardware: our own laptops; no special hardware.

How it is creative

  • It answers "is it real?" and not only "what changed?" Every trend comes with a significance test written in plain words.
  • Several views of the same question: a time series, a hotspot map, a comparison of regions and variables, and a forecast, all from one place and variable.
  • Natural-language entry: you type a question and the tool builds the analysis plan. If the AI service is down, a keyword parser takes over, so the app keeps working.
  • The forecast has to earn its place: a model is shown only if it beats simple rules.

Factors our team considered

  • Scientific honesty.
    • Climate data move up and down from season to season, so we test trends on yearly values and on monthly differences from normal.
    • We use robust tests and clearly say when a trend is not significant or the record is too short.
  • Speed and reliability.
    • Long satellite records are slow to download, so we added a per-year cache, a time estimate before each download, and a cancel button.
    • A ready-made demo dataset lets the app run offline.
  • Accessibility: plain language, a simple four-step flow, an AI chat button, and a light version that runs in the browser with no installation.
  • Cost and openness: free, open NASA and climate data, and free tiers for hosting and AI.
  • Security: API keys stay on the server and are never stored in the code.
  • Teamwork: the team brought together bioinformatics, data science, mathematics, epidemiology and computer science. The statistics, machine-learning and app parts were built as separate modules and then joined into one pipeline.
